vignette: Raj, a 68-year-old South Asian man, sat quietly in the corner of the café, his back pressed firmly against the wall. This habit had taken root over the years as a protective measure; it allowed him to see the entrance and anyone who might approach him. Since the traumatic event that had altered the course of his life, he had become acutely aware of his surroundings, leading to a heightened state of alertness. It was a skill cultivated from necessity, but it also served as a constant reminder of the vulnerability he felt, a vulnerability that had seeped into the very fabric of his being. Raj often found himself believing he was a lousy coper, convinced that his reactions to the trauma defined him. This belief led him to feel that any attempt to face his fears was futile, reinforcing his reliance on avoidance and self-harm as the only means to cope with his overwhelming emotional state. This belief in his inadequacy only deepened his reliance on maladaptive strategies, as he felt that without these behaviors, he would be utterly powerless to manage the emotional chaos within him. This belief weighed heavily on him, leading to a sense of helplessness that made him resort to self-harming behaviors as a misguided attempt to cope with the emotional pain he felt unable to manage. Raj had come to believe that if he could not control the overwhelming emotions within him, the only way to alleviate the pain was through self-harm, which he thought would provide a brief escape from his emotional turmoil. This negative appraisal weighed heavily on his heart, leading him to engage in self-harming behaviors, a misguided attempt to release the overwhelming feelings that consumed him. Raj believed that if he couldn't manage his emotions, the only way to cope was through self-harm, which he saw as a way to regain some semblance of control over the chaos within him. Each instance of self-harm reinforced his negative self-view, making him feel even more like a failure who couldn't cope without resorting to such drastic measures. The need to resort to self-harm for relief led him to conclude that he was weak, as it seemed that only through inflicting pain could he gain a temporary reprieve from his emotional turmoil. The physical pain provided a temporary distraction from the emotional turmoil, yet it only deepened his belief that he would never experience normal emotions again. The traumatic incident occurred years ago but remained vividly etched in Raj's mind. The conviction that he was marked by this experience led him to revisit those memories repeatedly, each recollection reinforcing the belief that he was weak and helpless. His negative self-appraisal made every intrusive thought feel like a confirmation of his inadequacy, heightening his sense of threat as he perceived the world as a place full of dangers he could not navigate. He often recalled the sounds-the muffled voices, the heavy thud of footsteps approaching, and the sudden silence that followed. Each time a memory surfaced, he could hear those sounds echoing in his head, forcing him to relive the fear and helplessness he had experienced. The resurfacing memories made Raj feel as if the danger he faced during the trauma was still present, amplifying his sense of threat and keeping him on edge. Each time a memory broke through, it brought with it a renewed sense of danger, making him feel hunted and as if the trauma was not just a past event but an ongoing reality. In response to these distressing memories, Raj often felt the urge to isolate himself, convinced that withdrawing from social situations would keep him safe from the painful emotions that threatened to overwhelm him. This avoidance strategy only served to heighten his sense of threat, as each withdrawal reinforced the idea that the world was indeed a dangerous place from which he needed to escape. To shield himself from the onslaught of these distressing memories, he found himself withdrawing from social situations, believing that if he stayed away from others, he could avoid the painful feelings that surfaced when he was reminded of the trauma. In doing so, he believed he was protecting himself from further emotional pain, though this strategy only deepened his sense of isolation and reinforced his belief that he was incapable of handling social interactions. This auditory recall was so visceral that it triggered a physical response; the pain returned in the same spots where he had felt it during the assault. These memories not only evoked physical pain but also deepened his negative self-appraisal, leading him to question his strength and resilience each time they resurfaced. The memories became entwined with his thoughts, reinforcing his negative appraisals about himself and his inability to articulate what had happened. Raj struggled to find words to describe the event, feeling more like an outsider in his own life, disconnected from the emotions that once defined him. Raj's heightened perception of threat was a constant companion. His belief that he was fundamentally flawed and vulnerable to danger meant that he approached the world with a sense of impending doom, as if every encounter could lead to catastrophe. He jumped at the slightest touch, flinching at unexpected contact, and had developed a tendency to monitor sounds in his home, listening intently for any sign of intrusion. The world outside felt perilous, and he was convinced that he could never return to a state of normalcy. This overwhelming sense of threat reinforced his belief that he was fundamentally flawed, further entrenching the negative appraisals that plagued him. Feeling that danger lurked around every corner, Raj adopted maladaptive strategies such as isolating himself and staying vigilant, convinced that by doing so, he could prevent any potential harm and maintain a sense of control over his life. Each unexpected noise sent his heart racing, a stark reminder of the chaos that had once invaded his life. The interplay between his memories and his perception of threat became a self-reinforcing cycle; the more he recalled the trauma, the more he felt the need to protect himself, and the more he believed he was permanently marked by his experiences. As he continued to engage in maladaptive strategies to shield himself, he found that these behaviors only confirmed his fears, reinforcing the negative appraisals he held about his own resilience and worth. In seeking to shield himself from these memories, he resorted to maladaptive strategies that only deepened his negative self-view, trapping him in a loop of distress and avoidance. His conviction that he was permanently vulnerable to danger only intensified this vigilance, making him feel as though every moment was fraught with potential threat, even in familiar settings. This constant state of hyper-vigilance led him to believe that he was incapable of feeling safe, further embedding his negative self-assessment and increasing his anxiety about the world around him. In seeking to escape the overwhelming sensations, Raj often isolated himself, fearing that being alone would lead him to confront the painful memories he so desperately wanted to avoid. Yet, in this isolation, he found his negative appraisals strengthening. The more he withdrew from social contact, the more he internalized the belief that he was unworthy of companionship and support, intensifying his feelings of inadequacy and despair. The more he withdrew, the more he felt he was confirming his belief that he was a burden to others, leading him to adopt maladaptive strategies like self-harm and avoidance. He often thought he was a burden to others, further entrenching his belief that he was an outsider. The maladaptive strategies he employed to cope with his distress-self-harm, avoidance of social situations, and the need to sit with his back against a wall-only reinforced his negative self-view. His avoidance of discussing the trauma meant that the memories remained unprocessed; he had been keeping them at a distance for so long that when they resurfaced, they felt more vivid and consuming than ever. He could not escape the loop of pain that seemed to define his existence. His reliance on avoidance only perpetuated his negative self-view, as he began to see himself as someone who needed to hide rather than engage, further entrenching the belief that he was fragile and broken. Now, sitting in the café, Raj was grappling with the relentless cycle that had become his life. He had finally decided to seek help, pushed by the desire to reclaim a sense of normalcy that felt increasingly elusive. His ongoing struggles with negative self-appraisals and memories made him fear that therapy might reveal just how deeply his issues ran, leading him to doubt whether he could ever truly heal. His greatest fear was that he might never be able to feel whole again, that he would remain trapped in the shadows of his past. Yet, he also held a flicker of hope-the hope that, through therapy, he might learn to navigate the memories that haunted him, find ways to cope that did not involve self-harm, and ultimately, begin to heal the wounds that had defined him for far too long.

Since the traumatic event that had altered the course of his life, he had become acutely aware of his surroundings, leading to a heightened state of alertness. It was a skill cultivated from necessity, but it also served as a constant reminder of the vulnerability he felt, a vulnerability that had seeped into the very fabric of his being. Raj often found himself believing he was a lousy coper, convinced that his reactions to the trauma defined him. This belief weighed heavily on him, leading to a sense of helplessness that made him resort to self-harming behaviors as a misguided attempt to cope with the emotional pain he felt unable to manage. Raj had come to believe that if he could not control the overwhelming emotions within him, the only way to alleviate the pain was through self-harm, which he thought would provide a brief escape from his emotional turmoil. This negative appraisal weighed heavily on his heart, leading him to engage in self-harming behaviors, a misguided attempt to release the overwhelming feelings that consumed him. Raj believed that if he couldn't manage his emotions, the only way to cope was through self-harm, which he saw as a way to regain some semblance of control over the chaos within him. The physical pain provided a temporary distraction from the emotional turmoil, yet it only deepened his belief that he would never experience normal emotions again. The traumatic incident occurred years ago but remained vividly etched in Raj's mind. He often recalled the sounds—the muffled voices, the heavy thud of footsteps approaching, and the sudden silence that followed. Each time a memory surfaced, he could hear those sounds echoing in his head, forcing him to relive the fear and helplessness he had experienced. The resurfacing memories made Raj feel as if the danger he faced during the trauma was still present, amplifying his sense of threat and keeping him on edge. In response to these distressing memories, Raj often felt the urge to isolate himself, convinced that withdrawing from social situations would keep him safe from the painful emotions that threatened to overwhelm him. To shield himself from the onslaught of these distressing memories, he found himself withdrawing from social situations, believing that if he stayed away from others, he could avoid the painful feelings that surfaced when he was reminded of the trauma. This auditory recall was so visceral that it triggered a physical response; the pain returned in the same spots where he had felt it during the assault. These memories not only evoked physical pain but also deepened his negative self-appraisal, leading him to question his strength and resilience each time they resurfaced. The memories became entwined with his thoughts, reinforcing his negative appraisals about himself and his inability to articulate what had happened. Raj struggled to find words to describe the event, feeling more like an outsider in his own life, disconnected from the emotions that once defined him. Raj's heightened perception of threat was a constant companion. He jumped at the slightest touch, flinching at unexpected contact, and had developed a tendency to monitor sounds in his home, listening intently for any sign of intrusion. The world outside felt perilous, and he was convinced that he could never return to a state of normalcy. This overwhelming sense of threat reinforced his belief that he was fundamentally flawed, further entrenching the negative appraisals that plagued him. Feeling that danger lurked around every corner, Raj adopted maladaptive strategies such as isolating himself and staying vigilant, convinced that by doing so, he could prevent any potential harm and maintain a sense of control over his life. Each unexpected noise sent his heart racing, a stark reminder of the chaos that had once invaded his life. The interplay between his memories and his perception of threat became a self-reinforcing cycle; the more he recalled the trauma, the more he felt the need to protect himself, and the more he believed he was permanently marked by his experiences. In seeking to shield himself from these memories, he resorted to maladaptive strategies that only deepened his negative self-view, trapping him in a loop of distress and avoidance. His conviction that he was permanently vulnerable to danger only intensified this vigilance, making him feel as though every moment was fraught with potential threat, even in familiar settings. In seeking to escape the overwhelming sensations, Raj often isolated himself, fearing that being alone would lead him to confront the painful memories he so desperately wanted to avoid. Yet, in this isolation, he found his negative appraisals strengthening. The more he withdrew, the more he felt he was confirming his belief that he was a burden to others, leading him to adopt maladaptive strategies like self-harm and avoidance. He often thought he was a burden to others, further entrenching his belief that he was an outsider. The maladaptive strategies he employed to cope with his distress—self-harm, avoidance of social situations, and the need to sit with his back against a wall—only reinforced his negative self-view. His avoidance of discussing the trauma meant that the memories remained unprocessed; he had been keeping them at a distance for so long that when they resurfaced, they felt more vivid and consuming than ever. He could not escape the loop of pain that seemed to define his existence. Now, sitting in the café, Raj was grappling with the relentless cycle that had become his life. He had finally decided to seek help, pushed by the desire to reclaim a sense of normalcy that felt increasingly elusive. His greatest fear was that he might never be able to feel whole again, that he would remain trapped in the shadows of his past. Yet, he also held a flicker of hope—the hope that, through therapy, he might learn to navigate the memories that haunted him, find ways to cope that did not involve self-harm, and ultimately, begin to heal the wounds that had defined him for far too long.
